question: What is the meaning of bill of materials in relation to products and materials?
description: A Bill of Materials (BoM) is a comprehensive list that includes all the subassemblies, intermediates, parts, and raw materials required to create a parent assembly. It shows the quantities of each component needed for assembly. The BoM primarily supports a firm's material requirements planning and optimized production processes. It differs from other concepts by focusing on product information provided during design or assembly, rather than being a registration that occurs over the entire life cycle of a specific product.

3.5. Closely related concepts 
A number of concepts have thematic connections to, or overlap with 
passports. We explain four concepts to better understand how to 
distinguish from them, and to understand the relationships among them. 
• Bill of Materials (BoM): is ”a listing of all the subassemblies, in­
termediates, parts, and raw materials that go into a parent assembly 
showing the quantity of each required to make an assembly.” 
(Blackstone, 2013). 
A BoM is different in three key aspects. First, a BoM typically aims to 
support a firm’s material requirements planning and optimized pro­
duction (Stonebraker, 1996) (some exceptions (De Benedetto and 
Klemeˇs, 2010; Soust-Verdaguer et al., 2017)), where passports support 
multiple stakeholders in CE decision making (Honic et al., 2019d; 
Rudolphi, 2018). Second, a BoM registers subassemblies, intermediates, 
parts, raw materials, and their quantities (Blackstone, 2013), while a 
passport is more extensive (e.g., quality characteristics, disassembly 
guides, eco-certificates). Finally, a BoM holds product information 
provided upon design or assembly by the manufacturer (Stonebraker, 
1996), while a passport is a registration that takes place over the life 
cycle of a uniquely identifiable product.  
• Product Life cycle Management (PLM): is ”the business activity of 
managing, in the most effective way, a company’s products all the 
way across their life cycles; from the very first idea for a product all 
the way through until it is retired and disposed of” Stark (2015). 
There are two key differences between a PLM system and a passport. 
First, a PLM system supports more (core) functions than CE decision 
making only (e.g., fault diagnoses, material planning, production 
configuration and optimization). Second, a PLM system follows a 
different viewpoint regarding data registration and ownership. While a 
PLM system is considered a manufacturer’s business activity that sup­
ports the extended enterprise (e.g., customers, designers, suppliers) 
(Stark, 2015), a passport is an overarching entity with transferable 
ownership and data access under license to a variety of stakeholders 
regardless of where data resides. 
• Digital twin: is ”an integrated multi-physics, multi-scale, probabi­
listic simulation of a complex product and uses the best available 
physical models, sensor updates, etc., to mirror the life of its corre­
sponding twin. Meanwhile, digital twin consists of three parts: 
physical product, virtual product, and connected data that tie the 
physical and virtual product.” (Glaessgen and Stargel, 2012). 
The key of a digital twin is to mirror the real-time state of a physical 
object in a virtual environment for simulation purposes in order to 
optimize the object or its supply chain management (e.g., improved 
design, resource planning, manufacturing efficiency) (He and Bai, 
2020). Its typical focus is on optimizing the use phase by making use of 
the Internet of Things (IoT) (Verdouw et al., 2021). Some passports can 
be considered a digital twin as they provide a tool set for simulating 
different environmental scenarios of a product, but there are also 
numerous examples that do not simulate, nor use IoT technology. 
Furthermore, a digital twin can capture information about any physical 
entity, which can be a product such as in passports, but it may also be a 
process (e.g., to monitor the real-time status of a production line (Krit­
zinger et al., 2018; Stothard et al., 2019) or for farm control (Verdouw 
et al., 2021)). Finally, most reported digital twins consider, similar as in 
PLM, the twin as a manufacturer’s business activity that supports the 
extended enterprise (He and Bai, 2020; Tao et al., 2018).
